content: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent and serious condition in patients admitted to intensive care units (ICUs), often leading to significant morbidity and mortality. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is a blood purification method used to manage severe AKI, but its efficacy remains uncertain. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of different intensities of CRRT—intensive (≥35 mL/kg/h) versus less intensive (<35 mL/kg/h)—on mortality rates and kidney function recovery in critically ill patients with AKI. A systematic search was conducted up to February 9, 2016, using databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, as well as clinical trial registries. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, and data were independently extracted by two authors. Statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model, with results expressed as risk ratios (RR) for categorical outcomes and mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes, along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Six studies involving 3185 participants were included in the analysis. The studies were assessed as having low or unclear risk of bias. The findings revealed no significant difference in mortality risk between intensive and less intensive CRRT at 30 days (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.08) or beyond 30 days post-randomization (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.06). Similarly, there was no significant difference in the proportion of patients who were free of renal replacement therapy (RRT) after CRRT discontinuation (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.37) or among survivors at 30 days (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.11) and 90 days (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.01). The duration of hospital stay (MD -0.23 days, 95% CI -3.35 to 2.89) and ICU stay (MD -0.58 days, 95% CI -3.73 to 2.56) did not differ significantly between the two CRRT intensities. However, intensive CRRT was associated with a higher risk of hypophosphatemia (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.31). There was no significant difference in the occurrence of adverse events between the two groups (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.61). Subgroup analysis revealed that intensive CRRT reduced mortality risk in patients with post-surgical AKI (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.88), but this effect was not observed in other subgroups. In conclusion, the current evidence, which is of low quality, does not support a mortality or kidney function recovery benefit from more intensive CRRT in critically ill AKI patients. However, intensive CRRT increases the risk of hypophosphatemia and may reduce mortality in patients with post-surgical AKI. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify these findings.
